claims.text: A dense Cr2O3 passive film provides corrosion resistance in stainless and Fe-Cr steels.
The Cr2O3 passive film in these steels is thin, stable, and capable of continual repair.
A high density of grain boundaries provides rapid diffusion pathways for Cr from the steel bulk to the surface.
Grain-boundary-assisted Cr transport replenishes surface Cr and offsets passive-film loss in aggressive environments.
A Cr content of at least approximately 12 wt.% is sufficient for the proposed passivation mechanism.
Tens to hundreds of hours of exposure are sufficient to observe passive-film stabilization or degradation under the proposed test conditions.
Under corrosive conditions, Cr in the steel oxidizes preferentially to form Cr2O3.
Increasing grain-boundary density accelerates Cr diffusion sufficiently to repair disruptions in the passive film.
Rapid passive-film repair maintains low dissolution rates of the base metal.
Fine-grained steel will develop a thicker, more uniform, and more stable Cr2O3 passive film than coarse-grained steel of the same composition.
Fine-grained steel will exhibit lower corrosion-current density than the coarse-grained baseline.
Fine-grained steel will exhibit higher electrochemical impedance than the coarse-grained baseline.
The proposed grain-size effect should hold in moderately aggressive chloride-containing or acidic aqueous solutions and under chemical-processing or nuclear-coolant temperature and pressure regimes.
The proposed mechanism may not govern when stress-corrosion cracking, high mechanical loads, or irradiation effects dominate degradation.
Additional alloying elements such as Mo or Mn may alter passive-film repair and corrosion outcomes.
The quantitative dependence of passive-film repair rate and corrosion-rate reduction on grain size remains undetermined.
